chunks: "The C rating tells you how much current a battery can deliver, as a multiple of its capacity.
One C is the current that would drain the battery in one hour, so for a 2200 milliamp-hour pack, 1C is 2. 2 amps, and a 30C rating means 30 times that, or 66 amps.
Time to empty is one over C, so 30C is two minutes. So the maximum current is just I max equals C times capacity in amp-hours.
Most hobby packs list two numbers: a continuous rating, and a higher burst rating that is valid only for a few seconds. The important thing is what limits it.
It's the internal resistance and the heat. At 66 amps through, say, 10 milliohms, the cell drops 0. 66 volts and dissipates 66 squared times 0.
01 equals 44 watts inside a small pouch. That heats it up fast, and above about 60 degrees you're damaging the cell.
So the C rating is really a statement that the manufacturer thinks the cell survives that current within a temperature and sag limit.
Also, those ratings aren't standardized, so I treat them as a rough guide, and I'd measure the voltage sag and the temperature at my actual load.
When picking a battery I take my peak current, divide by capacity to get the required C, and add margin, maybe 30 to 50 percent.
And charge rates are separate and much lower, typically 1C."
